claim: Mitochondrial transport in axons is critical for neural circuit health and function.
source: Mitochondrial transport in axons is critical for neural circuit health and function.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial function in neurons.

claim: actr10nl15 mutants carry a loss-of-function mutation in actr10, a member of the dynein-associated complex dynactin.
source: This strain carries a loss-of-function mutation in actr10, a member of the dynein-associated complex dynactin.
evidence: The mutation was identified through RNAmapper analysis and confirmed through rescue experiments and TALEN-mediated disruption.

claim: Mitochondria fail to attach to the dynein retrograde motor in actr10 mutants.
source: In a genetic screen, we found a zebrafish strain in which mitochondria fail to attach to the dynein retrograde motor.
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial fractionation experiments showing loss of p150 from the mitochondrial fraction in actr10 mutants.

claim: The abnormal axon morphology and mitochondrial retrograde transport defects observed in actr10 mutants are distinct from dynein and dynactin mutant axonal phenotypes.
source: The abnormal axon morphology and mitochondrial retrograde transport defects observed in actr10 mutants are distinct from dynein and dynactin mutant axonal phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of actr10, dync1h1, and p150a/b mutants showing different axonal phenotypes.

claim: Actr10 lacking the dynactin binding domain maintains its ability to bind mitochondria.
source: In addition, Actr10 lacking the dynactin binding domain maintains its ability to bind mitochondria, arguing for a role for Actr10 in dynactin-mitochondria interaction.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mitochondrial fractionation experiments showing Actr10Δ7 in the mitochondrial fraction.

claim: Drp1 is implicated as a partner in Actr10-dependent mitochondrial retrograde transport.
source: Finally, genetic interaction studies implicated Drp1 as a partner in Actr10-dependent mitochondrial retrograde transport.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation showing Actr10-Drp1 interaction and genetic interaction experiments.

claim: Neurons use 4.7 billion molecules of ATP per second at rest.
source: It is estimated that at rest alone, neurons use 4.7 billion molecules of ATP per second (Zhu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from a published study (Zhu et al., 2012).

claim: Mitochondria regulate local calcium ion levels.
source: In addition to their critical role in cellular metabolism, mitochondria also regulate local calcium ion levels (Werth and Thayer, 1994).
evidence: This is cited from a published study (Werth and Thayer, 1994).

claim: High cytoplasmic calcium levels correlate with axonal degeneration.
source: During inactivity, this ion needs to be contained in intracellular compartments as high cytoplasmic calcium levels correlate with axonal degeneration (Avery et al., 2012; Vargas et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from multiple published studies.

claim: Mitochondrial motility is necessary to maintain mitochondrial health and function.
source: In addition to maintaining axon health, mitochondrial motility is also necessary to maintain mitochondrial health and function.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about mitochondrial dynamics.

claim: Interrupted mitochondrial fission or fusion has been linked to loss of mitochondrial DNA, loss of oxidative potential, and mitophagy.
source: Interrupted mitochondrial fission or fusion has been linked to loss of mitochondrial DNA, loss of oxidative potential, and mitophagy.
evidence: This is cited from a review (Scheibye-Knudsen et al., 2015).

claim: Mitofusin participates in the anterograde transport of mitochondria.
source: Mitofusin, an essential protein for mitochondrial fusion, participates in the anterograde transport of this organelle as well (Misko et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from a published study (Misko et al., 2010).

claim: Manipulation of Drp1 impacts the localization of mitochondria.
source: Furthermore, manipulation of the dynamin-like protein Drp1, necessary for mitochondrial fission, impacts the localization of mitochondria (Smirnova et al., 2001; Varadi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from published studies.

claim: Kinesin-1 attaches to mitochondria via the proteins Miro and Milton.
source: The primary anterograde mitochondrial motor, Kinesin-1, attaches to mitochondria via the proteins Miro (RhoT1/2; Guo et al., 2005) and Milton (TRAK1/2; Glater et al., 2006; Stowers et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from multiple published studies.

claim: Miro contains calcium sensitive EF hands that change conformation when exposed to high levels of calcium, resulting in the uncoupling of the Kinesin-1 motor from microtubules.
source: Miro contains calcium sensitive EF hands that, when exposed to high levels of this ion, change their confirmation, resulting in the uncoupling of the Kinesin-1 motor from microtubules (Saotome et al., 2008; Wang and Schwarz, 2009).
evidence: This is cited from published studies.

claim: Loss of Miro or Milton impacts anterograde and retrograde mitochondrial movement.
source: The Miro/Milton transport machinery is not specific for anterograde transport, however, as loss of either protein impacts anterograde and retrograde mitochondrial movement (Guo et al., 2005; Saotome et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from published studies.

claim: Retrograde mitochondrial transport depends on the cytoplasmic dynein complex.
source: Retrograde mitochondrial transport is known to depend on the cytoplasmic dynein complex (Pilling et al., 2006; Schnapp and Reese, 1989).
evidence: This is cited from published studies.

claim: Dynactin's p150 subunit facilitates dynein processivity and serves as an anchor for dynein at microtubule plus ends.
source: Dynactin, specifically its p150 subunit, has been shown to facilitate dynein processivity and also serves as an anchor for dynein at microtubule plus ends, facilitating cargo loading (Lloyd et al., 2012; Moughamian and Holzbaur, 2012; Schroer, 2004).
evidence: This is cited from published studies.

claim: The dynactin accessory complex is attached to dynein through interaction of p150 with the tails of the dynein intermediate chains.
source: The dynactin accessory complex is attached to dynein through interaction of p150 with the tails of the dynein intermediate chains (Vaughan and Vallee, 1995).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: Actr10 is part of the dynactin pointed end complex which is predicted to be in an ideal location for cargo binding.
source: Together with p25, p62 and p27, Actr10 is a part of the dynactin pointed end complex which is predicted to be in an ideal location for cargo binding (Yeh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: One key function for Actr10 is capping the actin-like Arp1 filament to regulate filament length and facilitate attachment of other pointed end proteins.
source: Structural work suggests that one key function for Actr10 is capping the actin-like Arp1 filament, to regulate filament length and facilitate attachment of other pointed end proteins (Urnavicius et al., 2015)
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: actr10nl15 mutants display axon terminal swellings in the central and peripheral nervous systems indicative of retrograde transport abnormalities.
source: actr10nl15 mutants (hereafter referred to as actr10) display axon terminal swellings in the central and peripheral nervous systems indicative of retrograde transport abnormalities.
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging of pLL axons in mutants.

claim: Mitochondria cluster at microtubule plus ends in actr10 mutants due to failed retrograde mitochondrial movement.
source: Analysis of cargo localization and movement in the actr10 mutant revealed clustering of mitochondria, but not other cargos analyzed, at microtubule plus ends due to failed retrograde mitochondrial movement.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging and kymograph analysis of mitochondrial transport.

claim: Abnormal mitochondrial movement in actr10 mutants is due to failed attachment of mitochondria to the dynein-dynactin complex.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that abnormal mitochondrial movement in actr10 mutants is due to failed attachment of mitochondria to the dynein-dynactin complex in the absence of Actr10.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mitochondrial fractionation experiments.

claim: pLL axons develop early with axon extension complete by 2 days post-fertilization and synapse formation occurring by 4 dpf.
source: pLL axons develop early (axon extension is complete by 2 days post-fertilization (dpf) and synapse formation occurs by 4 dpf)
evidence: This is cited from published studies on the zebrafish lateral line system.

claim: RNAmapper analysis identified the causal mutation as a single nucleotide change (T to G) in the start codon of actr10.
source: RNAmapper analysis (Miller et al., 2013) identified the causal mutation as a single nucleotide change (T to G) in the start codon of actr10.
evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing and mapping analysis.

claim: TALEN-mediated disruption of the first exon of actr10 phenocopied the mutant axon terminal swellings.
source: We confirmed actr10 as the affected gene using RNA-mediated rescue of axon terminal swellings and by performing TALEN- (Transcription Activator Like Effector Nuclease) mediated disruption of the first exon of actr10, which phenocopied the mutant axon terminal swellings
evidence: This is demonstrated through TALEN injection experiments and phenotypic analysis.

claim: Cytochrome c accumulates in actr10 mutant axon terminals.
source: This revealed an accumulation of Cytochrome c, a mitochondrial protein, in actr10 axon terminals (Figure 2A,B,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunolabeling experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: actr10 mutants display mitochondrial accumulation in pLL axon terminals.
source: actr10 mutants displayed mitochondrial accumulation in pLL axon terminals (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through live imaging of mitochondria labeled with TagRFP.

claim: Lamp1 and pJNK do not accumulate in actr10 mutant axon terminals.
source: Other known pLL axon retrograde cargos, including those labeled by Lamp1 (Lysosome associated membrane protein-1; late endosome/lysosome marker) and phosphorylated c-Jun N-Terminal Kinase (pJNK) did not accumulate (Figure 2F–K; Drerup and Nechiporuk, 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunolabeling experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Expression of wildtype Actr10 rescues mitochondrial accumulation in actr10 mutants.
source: Expression of wildtype Actr10 using zygotic injection of in vitro synthesized mRNA rescued mitochondrial accumulation in actr10 mutants (Figure 2L–O), confirming that Actr10 is necessary for proper mitochondrial positioning.
evidence: This is demonstrated through rescue experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mitochondria are highly enriched in the axon terminal swellings of actr10 mutants compared to other intracellular structures.
source: This experiment demonstrated mitochondria are highly enriched in the axon terminal swellings of actr10 mutants compared to other intracellular structures (Figure 3A,B; n = 3 wildtypes, n = 4 mutants).
evidence: This is demonstrated through TEM analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is a 37% reduction in the distance moved by mitochondria in the anterograde direction in actr10 mutants.
source: Kymograph analysis demonstrated a 37% and 39% reduction in the distance moved by mitochondria in the anterograde and retrograde directions respectively in actr10 mutants but no change in mitochondrial transport velocity (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through kymograph analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is a 39% reduction in the distance moved by mitochondria in the retrograde direction in actr10 mutants.
source: Kymograph analysis demonstrated a 37% and 39% reduction in the distance moved by mitochondria in the anterograde and retrograde directions respectively in actr10 mutants but no change in mitochondrial transport velocity (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through kymograph analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The frequency of anterograde mitochondrial transport is unchanged in actr10 mutants.
source: Despite the decrease in anterograde transport distance, the frequency of anterograde mitochondrial transport was unchanged in actr10 mutants.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of mitochondrial transport data.

claim: The frequency of retrograde mitochondrial transport is dramatically decreased in actr10 mutants.
source: In contrast, both the frequency of retrograde mitochondrial transport and the proportion of mitochondria moving in the retrograde direction were dramatically decreased in actr10 mutants (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of mitochondrial transport data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The proportion of mitochondria moving in the retrograde direction is dramatically decreased in actr10 mutants.
source: In contrast, both the frequency of retrograde mitochondrial transport and the proportion of mitochondria moving in the retrograde direction were dramatically decreased in actr10 mutants (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of mitochondrial transport data shown in Figure 4.

claim: actr10 is ubiquitously expressed, albeit enriched in the nervous system during larval stages.
source: actr10 is ubiquitously expressed, albeit enriched in the nervous system during larval stages (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through in situ hybridization shown in Figure 5.

claim: Neuronal expression of mRFP-Actr10 rescues axon terminal morphology and mitochondrial localization in actr10 mutants.
source: While mRFP-Actr10 expression in wildtype axons had no apparent effects (Figure 5D; n = 6 in 3 biological replicates), it rescued axon terminal morphology and mitochondrial localization in all mutants analyzed (Figure 5E–G; n = 5 mutants in 3 biological replicates).
evidence: This is demonstrated through rescue experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Actr10 functions autonomously in neurons to regulate axon morphology and mitochondrial localization.
source: These experiments confirmed a neuron-specific function for Actr10 in mitochondrial localization in axons.
evidence: This is demonstrated through neuron-specific rescue experiments.

claim: Neither Dynein heavy chain nor p150 are significantly mislocalized in actr10 mutant axons.
source: Neither Dynein heavy chain (DHC) nor p150 were significantly mislocalized in actr10 mutants, though we did observe a trend of increased DHC in actr10 mutant axon terminals (Figure 6A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunolabeling experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: There is no change in the parameters of retrograde dynein movement in actr10 mutants.
source: Kymograph analysis revealed no change in the parameters of retrograde dynein movement, though we did note a 42% reduction in the distance and a 26% reduction in the velocity of anterograde dynein transport.
evidence: This is demonstrated through kymograph analysis of dynein transport.

claim: There is a 42% reduction in the distance of anterograde dynein transport in actr10 mutants.
source: Kymograph analysis revealed no change in the parameters of retrograde dynein movement, though we did note a 42% reduction in the distance and a 26% reduction in the velocity of anterograde dynein transport.
evidence: This is demonstrated through kymograph analysis of dynein transport.

claim: There is a 26% reduction in the velocity of anterograde dynein transport in actr10 mutants.
source: Kymograph analysis revealed no change in the parameters of retrograde dynein movement, though we did note a 42% reduction in the distance and a 26% reduction in the velocity of anterograde dynein transport.
evidence: This is demonstrated through kymograph analysis of dynein transport.

claim: There is no change in the proportion of dynein-positive puncta moving in the anterograde or retrograde direction in actr10 mutants at 4 dpf.
source: Despite these defects in anterograde dynein transport, there was no change in the proportion of dynein-positive puncta moving in the anterograde or retrograde direction in actr10 mutants at 4 dpf (Figure 6I–M).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of dynein transport data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Loss of Actr10 does not impede dynein-dynactin complex localization or dynein retrograde movement in axons.
source: These experiments demonstrated that loss of Actr10 does not impede dynein-dynactin complex localization or dynein retrograde movement in axons.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunolabeling and live imaging experiments.

claim: i2b-GFP can integrate into the core dynein complex.
source: i2b-GFP can integrate into the core dynein complex (Figure 6N).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Loss of Actr10 does not impact dynein-dynactin interaction.
source: Western blot of larval extracts revealed no change in p150 interaction with the core dynein motor (Figure 6O). Together, these experiments confirmed that loss of Actr10 does not impact dynein-dynactin interaction.
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: There are small changes in anterograde transport velocity and distance of retrograde transport bouts of peroxisomes in actr10 mutants.
source: Kymograph analysis of peroxisome transport at 4 dpf demonstrated small changes in anterograde transport velocity and distance of retrograde transport bouts (Figure 7A–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through kymograph analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Lamp1-labeled vesicles are transported normally in actr10 mutant axons.
source: Analysis of Lamp1-positive vesicle movement at 4 dpf demonstrated that this cargo is transported normally in actr10 mutant axons (Figure 7H–L).
evidence: This is demonstrated through live imaging and kymograph analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Loss of Actr10 does not hinder the transport of all dynein-dependent, retrograde cargos in axons.
source: These live imaging experiments, in conjunction with the immunolabeling of known retrograde cargos (Figure 2) and our TEM studies (Figure 3), argue that loss of Actr10 does not hinder the transport of all dynein-dependent, retrograde cargos in axons.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: dync1h1 mutants display rapid degeneration of pLL axons by 4 dpf.
source: Unlike actr10 mutants (see Figure 1), dync1h1 mutants displayed rapid degeneration of pLL axons by 4 dpf, with pLL nerves extending less than half-way to the tail at this time-point (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging of dync1h1 mutants shown in Figure 8.

claim: Mitochondria accumulate in distal axons of dync1h1 mutants.
source: Mitochondria do accumulate in distal axons of dync1h1 mutants, as expected with global disruption of retrograde transport (Figure 8F,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging shown in Figure 8.

claim: The disparity between actr10 and dync1h1 mutant axonal phenotypes argues that loss of Actr10 does not impact all dynein function in axons.
source: The disparity between actr10 and dync1h1 mutant axonal phenotypes argues that loss of Actr10 does not impact all dynein function in axons.
evidence: This is inferred from comparative phenotypic analysis.

claim: There are two orthologs of p150 in zebrafish, p150a and p150b.
source: There are two orthologs of p150 in zebrafish, p150a and p150b.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of zebrafish.

claim: p150b is enriched in developing and mature neurons while p150a is enriched only in mature neurons.
source: These paralogues are highly similar at the amino acid level but have slightly different expression patterns: while both are ubiquitously expressed, p150b is enriched in developing (1 and 2 dpf) and mature (4 dpf) neurons while p150a is enriched only in mature neurons 4 dpf (Figure 9A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through in situ hybridization shown in Figure 9.

claim: Loss of p150a alone has no discernable effect on axons or mitochondrial localization.
source: Loss of p150a alone has no discernable effect on axons or mitochondrial localization (Figure 8C,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging of p150a mutants shown in Figure 8.

claim: p150b single mutants are indistinguishable from wild-type siblings at 4 dpf, with normal axon terminals and no abnormalities in mitochondrial localization.
source: p150b single mutants are indistinguishable from wild-type siblings at 4 dpf, with normal axon terminals and no abnormalities in mitochondrial localization (Figure 8D,I).
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging of p150b mutants shown in Figure 8.

claim: p150a/b mutants are phenotypically similar to dync1h1 mutants, with truncated pLL axons and mitochondrial accumulation at axon ends.
source: Unlike single p150 mutants, p150a/b mutants are phenotypically similar to dync1h1 mutants, with truncated pLL axons and mitochondrial accumulation at axon ends (Figure 8E,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging of p150a/b mutants shown in Figure 8.

claim: actr10 mutants do not phenocopy the axon truncation phenotype of dynein or dynactin loss of function mutants.
source: This confirms the reliance of mitochondria on the dynein-dynactin complex for retrograde movement and demonstrates that actr10 mutants do not phenocopy the axon truncation phenotype of dynein or dynactin loss of function mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from comparative phenotypic analysis.

claim: p150a/b double mutants have an almost complete cessation of mitochondrial movement in the anterograde and retrograde directions.
source: Unlike loss of Actr10, p150a/b double mutants had an almost complete cessation of mitochondrial movement in the anterograde and retrograde directions (Figure 8N,O).
evidence: This is demonstrated through kymograph analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: There is a dramatic loss of mitochondria from the central portion of axons in p150a/b double mutants.
source: In addition, we noted a dramatic loss of mitochondria from the central portion of axons in p150a/b double mutants, likely because of the strong defect in anterograde mitochondrial transport (Figure 8P).
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantification shown in Figure 8.

claim: pJNK accumulates in p150a/b mutant axon terminals.
source: Furthermore, two cargos known to localize normally in actr10 mutants, pJNK and Lamp1 (see Figure 2), accumulate in in p150a/b mutant axon terminals (Figure 10A–D)
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunolabeling shown in Figure 10.

claim: Lamp1 accumulates in p150a/b mutant axon terminals.
source: Furthermore, two cargos known to localize normally in actr10 mutants, pJNK and Lamp1 (see Figure 2), accumulate in in p150a/b mutant axon terminals (Figure 10A–D)
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunolabeling shown in Figure 10.

claim: In actr10 mutants, p150 is largely lost from the mitochondrial fraction with a concomitant increase of p150 to the light fraction.
source: Strikingly, in actr10 mutants, p150 was largely lost from the mitochondrial fraction with a concomitant increase of p150 to the light fraction, which contains all cellular components not pelleted under low centrifugation speeds (Figure 11B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mitochondrial fractionation experiments shown in Figure 11.

claim: Actr10 is necessary for mitochondrial attachment to dynactin.
source: This result demonstrates the necessity of Actr10 for mitochondrial attachment to dynactin.
evidence: This is inferred from mitochondrial fractionation experiments.

claim: Separate protein domains exist in Actr10 which are necessary for interaction with dynactin and mitochondria.
source: mRFP-Actr10 and mRFP-Actr10△7, expressed using zygotic microinjection of respective mRNAs, were both present in the mitochondrial fractionation (Figure 11D,H; n = 2), arguing that separate protein domains exist in Actr10 which are necessary for interaction with dynactin and mitochondria.
evidence: This is inferred from mitochondrial fractionation experiments shown in Figure 11.

claim: Actr10 participates in mitochondrial attachment to the retrograde motor protein complex in neurons.
source: This data supports a role for Actr10 in binding mitochondria to dynactin for retrograde mitochondrial transport.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: A lysine to alanine mutation at amino acid 38 in Drp1 causes clustering of mitochondria in the perinuclear region of fibroblasts in a microtubule-dependent manner.
source: Specifically, a lysine to alanine mutation at amino acid 38 in Drp1 (mimicking a constitutively GDP-bound form) causes clustering of mitochondria in the perinuclear region of fibroblasts in a microtubule-dependent manner (Smirnova et al., 2001; Varadi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from published studies.

claim: Drp1 interacts with Actr10.
source: Using immunoprecipitation, we demonstrated that Drp1 interacts with Actr10, with strongly enhanced interaction between Actr10 and the Drp1K38A variant (Figure 12A; n = 3 replicates in independent experiments; (Smirnova et al., 2001, 1998).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 12.

claim: The K38A mutation in Drp1 strengthens the interaction between Drp1 and Actr10.
source: Using immunoprecipitation, we demonstrated that Drp1 interacts with Actr10, with strongly enhanced interaction between Actr10 and the Drp1K38A variant (Figure 12A; n = 3 replicates in independent experiments; (Smirnova et al., 2001, 1998).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 12.

claim: Expression of Drp1K38A-mRFP causes mitochondrial clustering in wildtype pLL neuron cell bodies.
source: In wild-type larvae, expression of Drp1K38A-mRFP caused mitochondrial clustering in the perinuclear region, phenotypically similar to the results observed in cultured fibroblasts (Figure 12B,C; Smirnova et al., 2001; Varadi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging experiments shown in Figure 12.

claim: Drp1K38A-mRFP expression does not alter mitochondrial localization in actr10 mutant pLL neurons.
source: In contrast, Drp1K38A-mRFP expression did not alter mitochondrial localization in actr10 mutant pLL neurons (Figure 12D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging experiments shown in Figure 12.

claim: Expression of Drp1K38A causes a substantial decrease in the number of mitochondria per micron in wildtype but not actr10 mutant axons.
source: Indeed, expression of Drp1K38A caused a substantial decrease in the number of mitochondria per micron in wildtype but not actr10 mutant axons (Figure 12F–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantification shown in Figure 12.

claim: The biochemical and genetic interaction between Actr10 and Drp1K38A support a model in which Drp1, in its GDP-bound state, modulates dynein-based mitochondrial localization via an Actr10-dependent mechanism.
source: Together, the biochemical and genetic interaction between Actr10 and Drp1K38A support a model in which Drp1, in its GDP-bound state, modulates dynein-based mitochondrial localization via an Actr10-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from biochemical and genetic interaction experiments.

claim: Actr10 is a mediator of retrograde mitochondrial transport.
source: Using genetics, immunolabeling, biochemistry, and in vivo imaging of cargo movement, we have identified Actr10 as a mediator of retrograde mitochondrial transport.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: In the absence of Actr10, mitochondrial retrograde transport frequency is selectively disrupted, leading to accumulation of this organelle in axon terminals.
source: In the absence of this dynactin pointed end protein, mitochondrial retrograde transport frequency is selectively disrupted, leading to accumulation of this organelle in axon terminals.
evidence: This is demonstrated through multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Actr10 is necessary for dynactin-dependent, retrograde transport of mitochondria in axons.
source: Together, our data argue that Actr10 is necessary for dynactin-dependent, retrograde transport of mitochondria in axons.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Actr10 could directly link mitochondria to dynactin or potentially facilitate this interaction through other dynactin pointed end proteins, such as p62.
source: Actr10 could directly link mitochondria to dynactin or potentially facilitate this interaction through other dynactin pointed end proteins, such as p62.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental data.

claim: p62 is predicted to rely on Actr10 for binding to the dynactin complex.
source: p62 is of particular interest in this regard as it is predicted to rely on Actr10 for binding to the dynactin complex (Urnavicius et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: Knockdown of Actr10 using siRNA in Cos7 cells resulted in dissociation of the dynactin complex pointed end.
source: In support of this role, knockdown of Actr10 using siRNA in Cos7 cells resulted in dissociation of the dynactin complex pointed end (Yeh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: Loss of Actr10 in fungi phenocopies the abnormal nuclear positioning observed with loss of dynein.
source: Additionally, studies in the fungi neurospora and aspergillus demonstrated that loss of Actr10 phenocopies the abnormal nuclear positioning observed with loss of dynein (Lee et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from published studies.

claim: Zebrafish actr10 mutants display the small eye phenotype observed in dync1h1 and p150a mutants.
source: Similarly, zebrafish actr10 mutants display the small eye phenotype observed in dync1h1 and p150a mutants (see Figure 8 and Del Bene et al., 2008; Insinna et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging and cited from published studies.

claim: Knockdown of Actr10 resulted in multipolar spindle formation in Cos7 cells.
source: Finally, similar to loss of p150, knockdown of Actr10 resulted in multipolar spindle formation in Cos7 cells (Yeh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: Actr10 has been shown to regulate Arp1-membrane interaction.
source: Indeed, Actr10 has been shown to regulate Arp1-membrane interaction (Clark and Rose, 2006)
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: The zebrafish eye phenotype in the p150a mutant is due to a defect in interkinetic nuclear migration.
source: and the zebrafish eye phenotype in the p150a mutant is due to a defect in interkinetic nuclear migration (Del Bene et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: Actr10 may modulate both Arp1 interaction with the nuclear membrane and mitochondria-dynactin binding in axons.
source: Therefore, rather than purely serving a stabilizing role for the dynactin complex, Actr10 may modulate both Arp1 interaction with the nuclear membrane and mitochondria-dynactin binding in axons.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental data and literature.

claim: A variant of Actr10 lacking the dynactin binding domain retains its ability to interact with mitochondria.
source: In addition, a variant of Actr10 lacking the dynactin binding domain retains its ability to interact with mitochondria, further substantiating a direct role for this protein in mitochondria-dynactin interaction.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mitochondrial fractionation experiments.

claim: Actr10 participates in mitochondrial attachment to the retrograde motor protein complex in neurons in addition to potentially facilitating Arp1 capping and nuclear positioning in other contexts.
source: Together, our data argue that Actr10 participates in mitochondrial attachment to the retrograde motor protein complex in neurons in addition to potentially facilitating Arp1 capping and nuclear positioning in other contexts.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The interaction between Drp1 and Actr10 in mitochondrial retrograde transport may provide a link between mitochondrial movement and mitochondrial fission.
source: The interaction between Drp1 and Actr10 in mitochondrial retrograde transport may provide a link between mitochondrial movement and mitochondrial fission.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental data.

claim: Drp1 has the unique ability to elicit mitochondrial localization to microtubule minus ends.
source: Originally, we investigated the role of Drp1 in retrograde mitochondrial transport as previous studies revealed the unique ability of this GTPase to elicit mitochondrial localization to microtubule minus ends (Smirnova et al., 2001, 1998).
evidence: This is cited from published studies.

claim: Mitofusin binds to the Miro-Milton complex and is necessary for mitochondrial movement.
source: Specifically, the fusion-related protein Mitofusin binds to the Miro-Milton complex and is necessary for mitochondrial movement (Misko et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: Loss of Mitofusin results in decreased anterograde and retrograde mitochondrial transport in cultured neurons.
source: Similar to Miro and Milton, loss of Mitofusin results in decreased anterograde and retrograde mitochondrial transport in cultured neurons (Misko et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: The inner mitochondrial membrane protein Opa1 does not participate in transport.
source: Interestingly, the inner mitochondrial membrane protein Opa1, also necessary for mitochondrial fusion, does not participate in transport (Misko et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: Eliminating mitochondrial fusion itself does not impact mitochondrial movement.
source: Thus, eliminating mitochondrial fusion itself does not impact mitochondrial movement; rather mitochondrial outer membrane proteins may have dual roles in fusion-fission dynamics and transport.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited study on Opa1.

claim: Drp1 translocates to mitochondria where it can bind to receptors Fis1 and Mff.
source: Drp1 translocates to mitochondria where it can bind to receptors Fis1 and Mff (LosonLosón et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: In its GTP-bound form, Drp1 oligomerizes, forming a constrictable collar necessary for fission during which GTP is exchanged for GDP.
source: In its GTP-bound form, it then oligomerizes, forming a constrictable collar necessary for fission during which GTP is exchanged for GDP (Ingerman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: A Drp1 variant incapable of binding GTP stimulates mitochondrial accumulation at the nuclear periphery.
source: We found that a Drp1 variant incapable of binding GTP stimulates mitochondrial accumulation at the nuclear periphery, linking fission with transport.
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging experiments.

claim: Upon the GTP-GDP transition, mitochondria undergo fission and Drp1 recruits the retrograde motor protein complex through interaction with Actr10 to facilitate separation of daughter mitochondria.
source: Nevertheless, given the intriguing data generated here, it is tempting to speculate that, upon the GTP-GDP transition, not only do mitochondria undergo fission but Drp1 also recruits the retrograde motor protein complex through interaction with Actr10 to facilitate separation of these daughter mitochondria.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental data.

claim: Actr10 is a crucial protein for mitochondrial interaction with the dynein-dynactin complex, regulating retrograde transport.
source: Our work identifies Actr10 as a crucial protein for mitochondrial interaction with the dynein-dynactin complex, regulating retrograde transport.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The role of Actr10 is specific and not due to a general loss of dynactin stability or dynein function.
source: In addition, we argue that the role of Actr10 is specific and not due to a general loss of dynactin stability or dynein function.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The ability of Actr10 to bind mitochondria in the absence of dynactin and the disparate nature of the actr10-dync1h1 and actr10-p150a/b mutant phenotypes in axons are the strongest pieces of evidence supporting a specific role for Actr10.
source: The strongest pieces of evidence supporting this assertion are the ability of Actr10 to bind mitochondria in the absence of dynactin and the disparate nature of the actr10-dync1h1 and actr10-p150a/b mutant phenotypes in axons.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their experimental data.

claim: Mitochondrial transport and dynamics have been implicated in neurological disorders.
source: As mitochondrial transport and dynamics have been implicated in neurological disorders, a more complete mechanistic understanding of their regulation will provide insight into disease pathology.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.
